M09-2-Application-Data-Import-Export

Author

Dia Kaewdee

Preparation

In this assignment, I practiced importing, cleaning, exporting, joining, and visualizing data from several different sources. I also organized my project using the folder structure provided in the GitHub repository and confirmed my results after each major data manipulation step.

# Load the packages needed for this assignment

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(openxlsx)
library(lubridate)
library(janitor)
library(naniar)
library(rvest)
library(stringr)
library(WDI)
library(countrycode)
library(haven)
library(labelled)
library(sjlabelled)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)

Question 1: Dealing with csv file

Q1.1

The original CSV file uses semicolons instead of commas, so I imported it using the appropriate process. After importing the data, I examined the variable types and converted the order_date variable into a Date format so the data would be ready for analysis.

item_csv <- read_delim(
  "data/items_ordered.csv",
  delim = ";",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(item_csv)
Rows: 32
Columns: 5
$ customerid <dbl> 10330, 10101, 10298, 10101, 10299, 10339, 10449, 10439, 101…
$ order_date <chr> "30/jun/99", "30/jun/99", "01/jul/99", "01/jul/99", "06/jul…
$ item       <chr> "Pogo stick", "Raft", "Skateboard", "Life Vest", "Parachute…
$ quantity   <dbl> 1, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 3, 4,…
$ price      <dbl> 28.00, 58.00, 33.00, 125.00, 1250.00, 4.50, 180.79, 25.50, …
item_csv <- item_csv |>
  mutate(
    order_date = dmy(order_date)
  )

item_csv

Q1.2

Next, I found the most expensive item in the dataset by identifying the maximum price and filtering the corresponding row.

# Find the most expensive item

most_expensive_item <- item_csv |>
  filter(price == max(price, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  select(item, price)

most_expensive_item
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  item      price
  <chr>     <dbl>
1 Parachute  1250

Question 2: Dealing with excel file

Q2.1

For this question, I imported the Excel version of the items ordered dataset and named it item_excel. I also examined the structure and printed the data to confirm that the Excel file imported correctly.

Q2.2

Next, I created a chart showing the count of item quantities ordered. I also created an images folder and saved the same chart as PNG, PDF, and JPEG files.

# Create an images folder if it does not already exist

dir.create("images", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Create a chart showing the count of quantity ordered

quantity_chart <- item_excel |>
  ggplot(aes(x = quantity)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(
    title = "Count of Item Quantities Ordered",
    subtitle = "Imported from the Excel file",
    x = "Quantity Ordered",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Print the chart
quantity_chart
# Save the chart in different file formats

ggsave("images/quantity_chart.png", quantity_chart, width = 7, height = 5)

ggsave("images/quantity_chart.pdf", quantity_chart, width = 7, height = 5)

ggsave("images/quantity_chart.jpeg", quantity_chart, width = 7, height = 5)

Question 3: Importing from the clipboard and cleaning NA’s or “–”

Q3.1

For this question, I copied the Key Executives table from the Disney Yahoo Finance profile page and imported it from the clipboard. After importing the data, I cleaned the column names and replaced missing values such as "N/A" and "--" with R’s NA values.

# Import the Key Executives table from the clipboard

dis_exec <- read.delim(
  "clipboard",
  sep = "\t",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Print the imported data
dis_exec
                                                 ratio_gdp_2016...
1                                                          filter(
2                                          !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
3                                              !is.na(population),
4                                                   !is.na(region)
5                                                             ) |>

7                                                             aes(
8                                              x = gdp_per_capita,
9                                               y = student_ratio,
10                                              size = population,
11                                               label = country.x
12                                                               )
13                                                             ) +

16                                                    method = lm,

19                                                             ) +

22                                               max.overlaps = 10
23                                                             ) +

27                                                           labs(
28     title = GDP Per Capita and Student/Teacher Ratio by Region,
29                           subtitle = Secondary education, 2016,
30                                 x = GDP Per Capita (log scale),
31                                      y = Student/Teacher Ratio,
32                                               size = Population
33                                                             ) +
34                                                 theme_minimal()
# Clean the column names
dis_exec_clean <- dis_exec |>
  clean_names()

# Replace "N/A" and "--" with proper missing values
dis_exec_clean <- dis_exec_clean |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~na_if(.x, "N/A")
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~na_if(.x, "--")
    )
  )

Q3.2

Next, I exported the cleaned Disney executive data as both a CSV file and an Excel file into the project’s data folder.

# Save the cleaned data as a CSV file

write_csv(
  dis_exec_clean,
  "data/dis_exec_clean.csv"
)

# Save the cleaned data as an Excel file

write.xlsx(
  dis_exec_clean,
  "data/dis_exec_clean.xlsx"
)

Question 4: Web scraping

Q4.1

For this question, I used web scraping to read the archived IMDb Top 250 movies page. I first saved the URL and then scraped the movie titles into a vector called top_movies.

# IMDb Top 250 URL

url <- "https://web.archive.org/web/20220201012049/https://www.imdb.com/chart/top/"

# Scrape the movie titles

top_movies <- url |>
  read_html() |>
  html_elements(".titleColumn a") |>
  html_text(trim = TRUE)

# Check the number of movies scraped
length(top_movies)

Q4.2

Next, I scraped the movie years from the same IMDb page. I cleaned the year values by removing the parentheses and converting the result into a numeric variable.

# Scrape the movie release years

year <- url |>
  read_html() |>
  html_elements(".secondaryInfo") |>
  html_text(trim = TRUE) |>
  str_remove_all("\\(") |>
  str_remove_all("\\)") |>
  as.numeric()

# Check the number of years scraped
length(year)

Q4.3

Finally, I scraped the IMDb ratings from the same page and converted them into numeric values so they can be used for sorting and analysis later.

# Scrape the IMDb ratings

rating <- url |>
  read_html() |>
  html_elements("td.ratingColumn.imdbRating strong") |>
  html_text(trim = TRUE) |>
  as.numeric()

# Check the number of ratings scraped
length(rating)
[1] 250

Question 6: Replacing values with NA

Data

data <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name,           ~x,  ~y,              ~z,
  "N/A",           1,   "N/A",           -100,
  "N A",           3,   "NOt available", -99,
  "N / A",         NA,  "29",            -98,
  "Not Available", -99, "25",            -101,
  "John Smith",    -98, "28",            -1
)

data

4 Not Available   -99 25             -101

# library(naniar)

Q6.1

Replace all elements with “N/A” with the proper missing value in R (e.g., “NA”) across all character variables.

# Replace "N/A" with NA

data_q61 <- data |>
  replace_with_na(
    replace = list(
      name = "N/A",
      y = "N/A"
    )
  )

data_q61

  name              x y                 z
  <chr>         <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>
1 <NA>              1 <NA>           -100
2 N A               3 NOt available   -99
3 N / A            NA 29              -98
4 Not Available   -99 25             -101
5 John Smith      -98 28               -1

Q6.2

For this question, I replaced all "N/A", "N A", and "N / A" values with missing values using each of the four replacement functions available in the naniar package.

Using replace_with_na()

data_replace <- data |>
  replace_with_na(
    replace = list(
      name = c("N/A", "N A", "N / A")
    )
  )

data_replace
# A tibble: 5 × 4
  name              x y                 z
  <chr>         <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>
1 <NA>              1 N/A            -100
2 <NA>              3 NOt available   -99
3 <NA>             NA 29              -98
4 Not Available   -99 25             -101
5 John Smith      -98 28               -1

Using replace_with_na_all()

data_all <- data |>
  replace_with_na_all(~ . %in% c("N/A", "N A", "N / A"))

data_all
# A tibble: 5 × 4
  name              x y                 z
  <chr>         <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>
1 <NA>              1 <NA>           -100
2 <NA>              3 NOt available   -99
3 <NA>             NA 29              -98
4 Not Available   -99 25             -101
5 John Smith      -98 28               -1

Using replace_with_na_if()

data_if <- data |>
  replace_with_na_if(
    is.character,
    ~ . %in% c("N/A", "N A", "N / A")
  )

data_if

  replace_with_na_at(
    .vars = c("name", "y"),

  )

Q6.4

My favorite function is replace_with_na_if() because it can replace missing values across an entire type of variable without having to list each column individually. I think it is the most flexible option and would be the easiest to use on larger datasets.

Question 7: Impact of GDP on student/teacher ratio

Q7.1

For this question, I imported the student/teacher ratio dataset from GitHub. I examined missing values, the years included in the dataset, and the distribution of indicators. Then I filtered the dataset to only include 2016 Secondary Education rows with non-missing student/teacher ratios.

)

Q7.2

Next, I used the WDI package to collect 2016 GDP per capita and population data. I also kept the region and ISO3 country code so the World Bank data could be joined with the student/teacher ratio dataset. I noticed that sometimes World Bank has issues which can affect how the HTML renders.

indicators_2016 <- WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = c(
    gdp_per_capita = "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD",
    population = "SP.POP.TOTL"
  ),
  start = 2016,
  end = 2016,
  extra = TRUE
) |>
  select(
    iso3c,
    country,
    region,
    gdp_per_capita,
    population
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(iso3c),
    !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
    !is.na(population)
  )

Q7.4

This chart compares GDP per capita with the student/teacher ratio. I mapped population to the size of the points and region to color so the relationship is easier to compare across countries.

ratio_gdp_2016 |>
  filter(
    !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
    !is.na(population),
    !is.na(region)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = gdp_per_capita,
      y = student_ratio,
      size = population,
      color = region,
      label = country.x
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    size = 2.5,
    max.overlaps = 20
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP Per Capita and Student/Teacher Ratio",
    subtitle = "Secondary education, 2016",
    x = "GDP Per Capita (log scale)",
    y = "Student/Teacher Ratio",
    color = "Region",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Q7.5

For the final chart in this question, I separated the GDP and student/teacher ratio relationship by region. This makes it easier to compare whether the pattern looks different across world regions.

ratio_gdp_2016 |>
  filter(
    !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
    !is.na(population),
    !is.na(region)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = gdp_per_capita,
      y = student_ratio,
      size = population,
      label = country.x
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    size = 2.2,
    max.overlaps = 10
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  facet_wrap(~region) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP Per Capita and Student/Teacher Ratio by Region",
    subtitle = "Secondary education, 2016",
    x = "GDP Per Capita (log scale)",
    y = "Student/Teacher Ratio",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Q8.3

Finally, I explored job-related technology ownership. I selected the technology variables, reshaped them into a longer format, and created a chart showing the count of people who use each product.

job_tech_count <- demo |>
  select(
    wireless,
    multline,
    voice,
    pager,
    internet,
    callid,
    callwait
  ) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), as_factor)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "technology",
    values_to = "ownership"
  ) |>
  filter(ownership == "Yes") |>
  count(technology, ownership)

job_tech_count
# A tibble: 0 × 3
# ℹ 3 variables: technology <chr>, ownership <fct>, n <int>
ggplot(job_tech_count, aes(x = reorder(technology, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Count of Job-Related Technology Ownership",
    subtitle = "Based on the demo.sav labelled dataset",
    x = "Technology Product",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Question 9: Impact of retirement on the use of the total job-related technology products

Q9.1

For this question, I created a new variable called total_job_tech. This variable counts how many job-related technology products each participant uses. Then I added a variable label to make the new variable easier to understand.

demo <- demo |>
  mutate(
    total_job_tech =
      as.numeric(as_factor(wireless) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(multline) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(voice) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(pager) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(internet) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(callid) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(callwait) == "Yes")
  )

var_label(demo$total_job_tech) <- "Total number of job-related technology products used"

demo |>
  select(
    wireless,
    multline,
    voice,
    pager,
    internet,
    callid,
    callwait,
    total_job_tech
  )

Q9.3

From these comparisons, employment-related variables do seem connected to job-related technology ownership. Participants who are not retired or who are more active in employment categories generally appear to use more job-related technology products. This makes sense because people who are still working are more likely to need tools such as internet, voicemail, multiple phone lines, and call-related services for their jobs.

Question 10: Job-related technology product ownership

Q10

For this question, I calculated the proportion of participants who own each job-related technology product. I then created a bar chart showing the proportions, added 95% confidence interval error bars, displayed the proportions on each bar, and ordered the products from the highest to the lowest ownership rate.

tech_summary <- demo |>
  select(
    wireless,
    multline,
    voice,
    pager,
    internet,
    callid,
    callwait
  ) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), ~ as_factor(.) == "Yes")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "technology",
    values_to = "ownership"
  ) |>
  group_by(technology) |>
  summarise(
    proportion = mean(ownership, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(ownership)),
    se = sqrt(proportion * (1 - proportion) / n),
    lower = proportion - 1.96 * se,
    upper = proportion + 1.96 * se
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion))

tech_summary$technology <-
  factor(
    tech_summary$technology,
    levels = tech_summary$technology
  )

ggplot(
  tech_summary,
  aes(
    x = technology,
    y = proportion
  )
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = lower,
      ymax = upper
    ),
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = scales::percent(
        proportion,
        accuracy = 0.1
      )
    ),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent,
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Ownership of Job-Related Technology Products",
    subtitle = "Proportion of participants owning each product (95% confidence intervals)",
    x = "Technology Product",
    y = "Proportion of Participants"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Question 1: Dealing with csv file

## Q1.1

The original CSV file uses semicolons instead of commas, so I imported it using the appropriate process. After importing the data, I examined the variable types and converted the `order_date` variable into a Date format so the data would be ready for analysis.

```{r}
item_csv <- read_delim(
  "data/items_ordered.csv",
  delim = ";",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(item_csv)

item_csv <- item_csv |>
  mutate(
    order_date = dmy(order_date)
  )

item_csv
```

## Q1.2

Next, I found the most expensive item in the dataset by identifying the maximum price and filtering the corresponding row.

```{r}
# Find the most expensive item

most_expensive_item <- item_csv |>
  filter(price == max(price, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  select(item, price)

most_expensive_item
```

# Question 3: Importing from the clipboard and cleaning NA's or "--"

## Q3.1

For this question, I copied the **Key Executives** table from the Disney Yahoo Finance profile page and imported it from the clipboard. After importing the data, I cleaned the column names and replaced missing values such as `"N/A"` and `"--"` with R's `NA` values.

```{r}
# Import the Key Executives table from the clipboard

dis_exec <- read.delim(
  "clipboard",
  sep = "\t",
  header = TRUE,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Print the imported data
dis_exec

# Clean the column names
dis_exec_clean <- dis_exec |>
  clean_names()

# Replace "N/A" and "--" with proper missing values
dis_exec_clean <- dis_exec_clean |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~na_if(.x, "N/A")
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.character),
      ~na_if(.x, "--")
    )
  )

# Print the cleaned data
dis_exec_clean
```

## Q3.2

Next, I exported the cleaned Disney executive data as both a CSV file and an Excel file into the project's `data` folder.

```{r}
# Save the cleaned data as a CSV file

write_csv(
  dis_exec_clean,
  "data/dis_exec_clean.csv"
)

# Save the cleaned data as an Excel file

write.xlsx(
  dis_exec_clean,
  "data/dis_exec_clean.xlsx"
)

# Print the cleaned data
dis_exec_clean
```

# Question 4: Web scraping

## Q4.1

For this question, I used web scraping to read the archived IMDb Top 250 movies page. I first saved the URL and then scraped the movie titles into a vector called `top_movies`.

```{r}
# IMDb Top 250 URL

url <- "https://web.archive.org/web/20220201012049/https://www.imdb.com/chart/top/"

length(top_movies)

top_movies
```

## Q4.2

Next, I scraped the movie years from the same IMDb page. I cleaned the year values by removing the parentheses and converting the result into a numeric variable.

```{r}
# Scrape the movie release years

year <- url |>
  read_html() |>
  html_elements(".secondaryInfo") |>
  html_text(trim = TRUE) |>
  str_remove_all("\\(") |>
  str_remove_all("\\)") |>
  as.numeric()

length(year)

year
```

Finally, I scraped the IMDb ratings from the same page and converted them into numeric values so they can be used for sorting and analysis later.

```{r}
rating
```

# Question 6: Replacing values with NA

## Data

```{r}
data <- tibble::tribble(
  ~name,           ~x,  ~y,              ~z,
  "N/A",           1,   "N/A",           -100,
  "N A",           3,   "NOt available", -99,
  "N / A",         NA,  "29",            -98,
  "Not Available", -99, "25",            -101,
  "John Smith",    -98, "28",            -1
)

data

# library(naniar)
```

## Q6.1

Replace all elements with "N/A" with the proper missing value in R (e.g., "NA") across all character variables.

```{r}
# Replace "N/A" with NA

data_q61 <- data |>
  replace_with_na(
    replace = list(
      name = "N/A",
      y = "N/A"
    )
  )

data_q61
```

## Q6.2

For this question, I replaced all `"N/A"`, `"N A"`, and `"N / A"` values with missing values using each of the four replacement functions available in the `naniar` package.

Using `replace_with_na()`

```{r}
data_replace <- data |>
  replace_with_na(
    replace = list(
      name = c("N/A", "N A", "N / A")
    )
  )

data_replace
```

Using `replace_with_na_all()`

```{r}
data_all <- data |>
  replace_with_na_all(~ . %in% c("N/A", "N A", "N / A"))

data_all
```

Using `replace_with_na_if()`

```{r}
data_if <- data |>
  replace_with_na_if(
    is.character,
    ~ . %in% c("N/A", "N A", "N / A")
  )

data_if
```

Using `replace_with_na_at()`

```{r}
data_at <- data |>
  replace_with_na_at(
    .vars = c("name", "y"),
    ~ . %in% c("N/A", "N A", "N / A")
  )

data_at
```

## Q6.3

Next, I replaced the values `-99` and `-98` with missing values using each of the four replacement functions.

Using `replace_with_na()`

```{r}
num_replace <- data |>
  replace_with_na(
    replace = list(
      x = c(-99, -98),
      z = c(-99, -98)
    )
  )

num_replace
```

Using `replace_with_na_all()`

```{r}
num_all <- data |>
  replace_with_na_all(~ . %in% c(-99, -98))

num_all
```

Using `replace_with_na_if()`

```{r}
num_if <- data |>
  replace_with_na_if(
    is.numeric,
    ~ . %in% c(-99, -98)
  )

num_if
```

Using `replace_with_na_at()`

```{r}
num_at <- data |>
  replace_with_na_at(
    .vars = c("x", "z"),
    ~ . %in% c(-99, -98)
  )

num_at
```

## Q6.4

My favorite function is `replace_with_na_if()` because it can replace missing values across an entire type of variable without having to list each column individually. I think it is the most flexible option and would be the easiest to use on larger datasets.

# Question 7: Impact of GDP on student/teacher ratio

## Q7.1

For this question, I imported the student/teacher ratio dataset from GitHub. I examined missing values, the years included in the dataset, and the distribution of indicators. Then I filtered the dataset to only include 2016 Secondary Education rows with non-missing student/teacher ratios.

```{r}
student_teacher_ratio <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2019/2019-05-07/student_teacher_ratio.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

glimpse(student_teacher_ratio)

# Check missing values by variable
student_teacher_ratio |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.))))

# Check years covered in the data
student_teacher_ratio |>
  count(year)

# Check indicators and their distribution
student_teacher_ratio |>
  count(indicator, sort = TRUE)

# Filter to 2016 Secondary Education with no missing student_ratio
s_t_ratio_2nd_edu_2016 <- student_teacher_ratio |>
  filter(
    year == 2016,
    indicator == "Secondary Education",
    !is.na(student_ratio)
  )

dim(s_t_ratio_2nd_edu_2016)

s_t_ratio_2nd_edu_2016
```

## Q7.2

Next, I used the `WDI` package to collect 2016 GDP per capita and population data. I also kept the region and ISO3 country code so the World Bank data could be joined with the student/teacher ratio dataset. I noticed that sometimes World Bank has issues which can affect how the HTML renders.

```{r}
indicators_2016 <- WDI(
  country = "all",
  indicator = c(
    gdp_per_capita = "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD",
    population = "SP.POP.TOTL"
  ),
  start = 2016,
  end = 2016,
  extra = TRUE
) |>
  select(
    iso3c,
    country,
    region,
    gdp_per_capita,
    population
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(iso3c),
    !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
    !is.na(population)
  )

glimpse(indicators_2016)

indicators_2016
```

When rendering this assignment, the World Bank API returned an HTTP 502 Bad Gateway error. The code follows the assignment instructions and uses the required `WDI` package, but the API was temporarily unavailable during execution.

## Q7.3

I joined the 2016 student/teacher ratio data with the 2016 World Bank indicators using the three-letter country code. Then I examined the distribution of `student_ratio` and created a log-transformed version of the histogram because the distribution has a long right tail.

```{r}
ratio_gdp_2016 <- s_t_ratio_2nd_edu_2016 |>
  left_join(
    indicators_2016,
    by = c("country_code" = "iso3c")
  )

glimpse(ratio_gdp_2016)

ratio_gdp_2016

# Examine the distribution of student_ratio
summary(ratio_gdp_2016$student_ratio)

ggplot(ratio_gdp_2016, aes(x = student_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Student/Teacher Ratio",
    x = "Student/Teacher Ratio",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(ratio_gdp_2016, aes(x = student_ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Student/Teacher Ratio",
    subtitle = "X-axis is log-transformed",
    x = "Student/Teacher Ratio (log scale)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Q7.4

This chart compares GDP per capita with the student/teacher ratio. I mapped population to the size of the points and region to color so the relationship is easier to compare across countries.

```{r}
ratio_gdp_2016 |>
  filter(
    !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
    !is.na(population),
    !is.na(region)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = gdp_per_capita,
      y = student_ratio,
      size = population,
      color = region,
      label = country.x
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    size = 2.5,
    max.overlaps = 20
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP Per Capita and Student/Teacher Ratio",
    subtitle = "Secondary education, 2016",
    x = "GDP Per Capita (log scale)",
    y = "Student/Teacher Ratio",
    color = "Region",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Q7.5

For the final chart in this question, I separated the GDP and student/teacher ratio relationship by region. This makes it easier to compare whether the pattern looks different across world regions.

```{r}
ratio_gdp_2016 |>
  filter(
    !is.na(gdp_per_capita),
    !is.na(population),
    !is.na(region)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = gdp_per_capita,
      y = student_ratio,
      size = population,
      label = country.x
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  geom_text_repel(
    size = 2.2,
    max.overlaps = 10
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = dollar_format()) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  facet_wrap(~region) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP Per Capita and Student/Teacher Ratio by Region",
    subtitle = "Secondary education, 2016",
    x = "GDP Per Capita (log scale)",
    y = "Student/Teacher Ratio",
    size = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Question 9: Impact of retirement on the use of the total job-related technology products

## Q9.1

For this question, I created a new variable called `total_job_tech`. This variable counts how many job-related technology products each participant uses. Then I added a variable label to make the new variable easier to understand.

```{r}
demo <- demo |>
  mutate(
    total_job_tech =
      as.numeric(as_factor(wireless) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(multline) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(voice) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(pager) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(internet) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(callid) == "Yes") +
      as.numeric(as_factor(callwait) == "Yes")
  )

var_label(demo$total_job_tech) <- "Total number of job-related technology products used"

demo |>
  select(
    wireless,
    multline,
    voice,
    pager,
    internet,
    callid,
    callwait,
    total_job_tech
  )
```

## Q9.2

Next, I created tables showing the average number of job-related technology products by retirement status, employment category, and job satisfaction.

```{r}
demo |>
  mutate(retire = as_factor(retire)) |>
  group_by(retire) |>
  summarise(
    average_total_job_tech = mean(total_job_tech, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )
```

```{r}
demo |>
  mutate(empcat = as_factor(empcat)) |>
  group_by(empcat) |>
  summarise(
    average_total_job_tech = mean(total_job_tech, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )
```

```{r}
demo |>
  mutate(jobsat = as_factor(jobsat)) |>
  group_by(jobsat) |>
  summarise(
    average_total_job_tech = mean(total_job_tech, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n()
  )
```

## Q9.3

From these comparisons, employment-related variables do seem connected to job-related technology ownership. Participants who are not retired or who are more active in employment categories generally appear to use more job-related technology products. This makes sense because people who are still working are more likely to need tools such as internet, voicemail, multiple phone lines, and call-related services for their jobs.

# Question 10: Job-related technology product ownership

## Q10

For this question, I calculated the proportion of participants who own each job-related technology product. I then created a bar chart showing the proportions, added 95% confidence interval error bars, displayed the proportions on each bar, and ordered the products from the highest to the lowest ownership rate.

```{r}
tech_summary <- demo |>
  select(
    wireless,

  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "technology",
    values_to = "ownership"
  ) |>
  group_by(technology) |>
  summarise(
    proportion = mean(ownership, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(ownership)),
    se = sqrt(proportion * (1 - proportion) / n),
    lower = proportion - 1.96 * se,
    upper = proportion + 1.96 * se
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion))

tech_summary$technology <-
  factor(

ggplot(
  tech_summary,

    x = technology,

) +

  geom_text(

```
